warmup.q: A ZGC log line says GC(3) Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 852M(83%)->176M(17%) 0.071s. How long were the application threads stopped?
options: About 0.05 ms in all, spread over three short pauses
Not at all: ZGC never stops threads
It depends on how much was freed: 676 MB takes longer
warmup.why: The 0.071 s on that line is the whole collection, which ran while the application kept working. The stops are the Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start lines: 0.011, 0.015 and 0.020 ms in that run, 0.046 ms together. ZGC does stop threads, just very briefly, and how much it frees doesn't change the pauses.

opening:
Back in the warehouse, the last lesson's crew, G1, had one habit nobody could miss. Every time it moved boxes, it called "pens down!", and every worker waited until the last box sat on its new shelf. On a small floor that takes a few milliseconds. On a floor with millions of boxes still in use, the wait grows with them.

Now picture a crew that moves boxes while the workers keep working. Each time it moves a box, it leaves a forwarding note: "this box is now on shelf 812". A worker who follows an old shelf number reads the note once and corrects their own notepad. That crew is ZGC.

Its log holds the first surprise. A line like Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 852M(83%)->176M(17%) 0.071s looks like a 71 ms stop, yet the threads stopped for less than a tenth of a millisecond. The easy trap comes next: lowest pauses, so use it everywhere.

In this lesson, we'll watch ZGC move boxes under the workers' feet, add up what that costs, meet Shenandoah, and choose a collector with a table. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a crew that moves boxes while the workers keep working. ZGC does it with colored references and a load barrier, and Shenandoah with a design of its own. Both pay in CPU and headroom, ZGC in bigger references too. G1 still suits most programs, and Epsilon measures them.

Now check a program of yours: which collector does it really run? Print the collector names with the compare block's three lines at startup, or run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside its container.

Next, we'll read the crew's logbook line by line, and fit the whole warehouse onto the plot a container gives it. Why can a program whose heap fits its memory limit still be killed without a word?

sections.h: Moving boxes while the workers keep working: how ZGC relocates
sections.html:
In lesson 4, almost all of a G1 young pause, the stop in which G1 cleans the area for new objects, was "Evacuate Collection Set": the collector copying live objects while every thread waited. (The heap is the memory where a Java program keeps its objects, the garbage collector is the part of the JVM that frees the objects nothing uses any more, and a thread is one path of work running through the program.) That pause grows with what survives. Give the thumbnail service a cache of many gigabytes, and every young pause has more to copy.

ZGC, the Z Garbage Collector, moves objects while your threads keep running. It has been ready for production since JDK 15. The hard part is easy to state: a thread may be about to follow a reference, an object's address, to an object the collector has just moved. ZGC handles that with two tricks.

The first trick is the colored pointer. Every reference stored in the heap carries a few extra bits, its color, which say whether the reference is up to date with the crew's current round of work. Picture a small colored sticker on every note. The bits need room, so ZGC doesn't use lesson 1's compressed 4-byte references: each one takes 8 bytes. Lesson 1's Thumbnail takes 40 bytes under G1 on JDK 25 and 48 under ZGC. The allocation counter says so: 10,000 thumbnails, 480,000 bytes.

The second trick is the load barrier: a few instructions added after every load of a reference from the heap. The JIT compiler puts them there; it's the part of the JVM, the program that runs your code, that turns busy bytecode into machine code. Here's what the barrier adds, in spirit:

thumb = cache.latest                        // the load you wrote
if (color(thumb) != GOOD)                   // the barrier: one test and one branch
    thumb = cache.latest = fix(thumb)       // rare: find the new address, repair the field

Nearly always the color is good, and the barrier costs a test and a branch. When it isn't, the object may have moved. The barrier looks up the new address, moves the object itself if the crew hasn't got to it yet, and writes the repaired reference back into the field. The next load from that field takes the fast path again. The worker reads the forwarding note once and fixes the shelf number for good.

Here the picture bends in two places, and both matter. ZGC doesn't leave its forwarding notes on the old shelves. It keeps them in a small table beside each area it empties, so the old shelves can take new boxes right away. And a real worker reads a forwarding note only after walking to an old shelf. ZGC's check runs on every reference load, all day, whether a move is going on or not.

What's left for the pauses is small and fixed: switching the crew from one step to the next. Since JDK 16, ZGC even scans the threads' stacks while they run (JEP 376). The java manual promises "max pause times of a few milliseconds" and says "pause times are independent of what heap size is used", for heaps from 8 MB to 16 TB.

The flags changed along the way. JDK 21 added generational ZGC, with lesson 4's young and old generations, as an option (-XX:+ZGenerational, JEP 439). JDK 23 made it the default (JEP 474), and JDK 24 removed the old single-generation mode (JEP 490). On JDK 25, -XX:+UseZGC means generational ZGC, which also has a barrier on reference stores to track notes from old boxes to young ones, the job G1's cards do.

Now read one collection from the log. These lines come from a JDK 25 run of the demo's load, logged with -Xlog:gc* and trimmed, on a 4-core machine busy with other work (ZGC's own log reported a load of 26):

GC(3) Minor Collection (Allocation Rate)
GC(3) y: Pause Mark Start 0.011ms
GC(3) y: Concurrent Mark 24.398ms
GC(3) y: Pause Mark End 0.015ms
GC(3) y: Concurrent Select Relocation Set 0.184ms
GC(3) y: Pause Relocate Start 0.020ms
GC(3) y: Concurrent Relocate 34.916ms
GC(3) Minor Collection (Allocation Rate) 852M(83%)->176M(17%) 0.071s

A minor collection cleans only the young generation, and y: marks its lines. The heap went from 852 MB used to 176 MB. The 0.071 s on the last line is the whole collection, which ran beside the application. The pauses are the three Pause lines, 0.046 ms together. Seventy-one milliseconds of cleaning, and the workers lost less than a twentieth of one.

So the pauses are nearly gone. The work isn't. Somebody still marks and moves every live box, and somebody runs that barrier.

try.title: Find the pauses in a ZGC log
steps: Read ZgcDemo. It runs two seconds of the stand-in thumbnail service from lesson 4 under ZGC with a 1 GB heap, in a child JVM (it adds -XX:+ZGenerational on JDK 21 and 22). Then it prints every line of the first minor collection and adds up the pauses.
Predict before you run: will the pauses be longer than G1's young pauses in lesson 4, about the same, or shorter? And the time on the collection's last line?
Run it, and match the three Pause lines to the three red marks in the figure.
Change -Xmx1g to -Xmx96m in the demo and run it again. Watch the last line.

code.title: ZgcDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l05; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import workbench.memory.l04.ServiceLoad; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** * Runs two seconds of service load under generational ZGC in a child JVM. Prints every line of the * first minor collection, then compares the real pauses with the collection times. */ public class ZgcDemo { static final Pattern PAUSE = Pattern.compile("Pause .*?([\\d.]+)ms$"); static final Pattern CYCLE = Pattern.compile("GC\\((\\d+)\\) (Minor|Major) Collection \\(.*\\) .*->.* ([\\d.]+)s$"); public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { ServiceLoad.run(2, 0.30); return; } List<String> flags = new ArrayList<>(List.of("-XX:+UseZGC", "-Xmx1g", "-Xlog:gc,gc+phases")); if (Runtime.version().feature() < 23) flags.add("-XX:+ZGenerational"); // generational is the default from 23 List<String> log = Jvm.lines(flags, ZgcDemo.class.getName(), "load"); String firstMinor = log.stream().filter(l -> l.contains("Minor Collection")).findFirst() .map(l -> l.substring(l.indexOf("GC("), l.indexOf(')', l.indexOf("GC(")) + 1)).orElse("none"); log.stream().filter(l -> l.contains(firstMinor + " ")).forEach(l -> System.out.println(l.replaceAll("\\s+", " "))); int collections = 0, pauses = 0, stalls = 0; double longestPause = 0, totalPause = 0, totalCycle = 0; for (String line : log) { Matcher p = PAUSE.matcher(line), c = CYCLE.matcher(line); if (p.find()) { pauses++; double ms = Double.parseDouble(p.group(1)); totalPause += ms; longestPause = Math.max(longestPause, ms); } if (c.find()) { collections++; totalCycle += Double.parseDouble(c.group(3)); } if (line.contains("Allocation Stall (")) stalls++; } System.out.printf("%n%d collections took %.3f s in all, running alongside the application%n", collections, totalCycle); System.out.printf("%d stop-the-world pauses took %.3f ms in all; the longest was %.3f ms%n", pauses, totalPause, longestPause); System.out.println("allocation stalls: " + stalls); } }

try.expect: One minor collection prints about a dozen lines. Three are pauses (y: Pause Mark Start, y: Pause Mark End, y: Pause Relocate Start) of a few hundredths of a millisecond; the others are concurrent phases of milliseconds. In the JDK 25 run behind this lesson, on a busy machine: 10 collections took 0.464 s in all, while 40 stop-the-world pauses took 0.614 ms in all; the longest was 0.023 ms, and allocation stalls: 0. With a 96 MB heap the crew can't keep up: about 200 collections in two seconds, and 22 to 30 allocation stalls. Your numbers will differ.

video.title: ZGC moves objects while threads run: colored references and a load barrier that fixes stale ones on the next load

sections.h: What short pauses cost: CPU, headroom and bigger references
sections.html:
The java manual is honest about the price: ZGC gives low pauses "at some throughput cost". Throughput is how much useful work a program gets done for each second of CPU. The bill comes in three parts.

The first part is CPU. Marking and moving run on GC threads beside your threads, and the barrier's slow path runs on your own threads. A container is a fenced-off part of a shared machine, with its own limits on CPU and memory (lesson 6 looks at one closely). In a container with 2 CPUs, ZGC's threads compete with your request threads exactly when the service is busiest.

The second part is headroom: free space for the objects your code creates while the crew works. In the collection above, the application allocated another 100 MB during those 71 ms. One major collection, which cleans the young and old generations together, even ended fuller than it began:

GC(9) Major Collection (Allocation Rate) 258M(25%)->272M(27%) 0.078s

If the floor fills before the crew finishes, ZGC has one choice left: it makes the threads that want memory wait. The log calls that an allocation stall. Squeeze the demo's load into a 96 MB heap, and JDK 25 printed 22 lines like this in one two-second run and 30 in the next:

[2.162s][info][gc       ] Allocation Stall (main) 0.895ms

A stall hurts more than a pause, because it hits exactly the threads doing the most work. Stalls should be zero. When they aren't, give ZGC more heap or more CPU.

The third part is memory. With 8-byte references, every object that holds references grows, like the thumbnail from 40 to 48 bytes. Compact object headers from lesson 1 win that back: with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders on JDK 25, the same thumbnail took 40 bytes under ZGC. Short pauses move the work; they don't remove it. Check where it went.

Shenandoah is OpenJDK's other concurrent collector, a second crew with its own design. It also marks and moves objects while your threads run, and it also has a barrier on reference loads that sends a thread to an object's new copy. One difference shows in its log: after moving, Shenandoah walks the heap and fixes every old reference, in a phase called Concurrent update references. One JDK 25 cycle had four pauses, the longest 0.309 ms. It keeps 4-byte compressed references, so the thumbnail stays at 40 bytes. Its default mode has one generation; a generational mode was experimental in JDK 24 and is a product feature in JDK 25 (-XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational, JEP 521). Not every vendor's JDK includes Shenandoah, so check that java -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -version starts before you plan on it.

Let's put all of them on one load. The demo runs one second of it under five collectors, with a 512 MB heap each. Two JDK 25 runs on the busy machine gave the same shape. Here's the first, in full:

collector             pauses    longest   all pauses   rounds   CPU ms
UseSerialGC               31    15.58ms      161.9ms     1550      670
UseParallelGC             13    49.90ms      243.3ms     1299      610
UseG1GC                   12    13.49ms      110.4ms     1394      680
UseZGC                    58     2.63ms        3.4ms     2311     1010
UseShenandoahGC           30     5.16ms        9.4ms     1522      880

Across both runs, Serial, Parallel and G1 stopped the threads for 110 to 245 ms in total, ZGC and Shenandoah for 1 to 10 ms. In the second run ZGC's longest pause was 0.03 ms, so the 2.63 ms above is the busy machine, where any thread can wait for a core. The two concurrent crews used the most CPU both times: about 1,000 and 900 ms, against 610 to 890 for the rest. Don't judge throughput by the rounds column, though. Serial's jumped from 1,550 to 2,377 between runs.

Every crew makes a different trade, then. To choose one, you need to know which part of the bill your program can least afford.

List.of("-XX:+UseZGC", "-XX:+ZGenerational") : List.of("-XX:+UseZGC"), List.of("-XX:+UseShenandoahGC")); System.out.printf("%-20s %7s %10s %12s %8s %8s%n", "collector", "pauses", "longest", "all pauses", "rounds", "CPU ms"); for (List<String> gc : collectors) { List<String> flags = new ArrayList<>(gc); flags.addAll(List.of("-Xmx512m", "-Xlog:gc,gc+phases")); List<String> log = Jvm.lines(flags, CollectorCompareDemo.class.getName(), "load"); String name = gc.get(0).replace("-XX:+", ""); // "-XX:+UseG1GC" -> "UseG1GC" String result = log.stream().filter(l -> l.startsWith("RESULT ")).findFirst().orElse(null); if (result == null) { System.out.printf("%-20s not in this JDK build%n", name); continue; } int pauses = 0; double longest = 0, total = 0; for (String line : log) { Matcher m = PAUSE.matcher(line); if (m.find()) { pauses++; double ms = Double.parseDouble(m.group(1)); total += ms; longest = Math.max(longest, ms); } } String[] r = result.split(" "); System.out.printf("%-20s %7d %8.2fms %10.1fms %8s %8s%n", name, pauses, longest, total, r[1], r[2]); } } }

try.expect: Serial, Parallel and G1 have pauses of several to tens of milliseconds and 100 to 250 ms of pauses in total; Parallel often has the single longest one (about 50 ms in the runs behind this lesson). Shenandoah's longest pause is well under a millisecond to a few milliseconds, and ZGC's is usually a few hundredths of a millisecond, with a few milliseconds of pauses in all. ZGC and Shenandoah use more CPU for the same second. On a busy machine any pause can stretch, and the rounds column is too noisy to judge throughput from one run.

sections.h: Choosing a crew by what hurts most: the default and a decision table
sections.html:
Before you choose, know what you get when you choose nothing. On JDK 21 to 26, the JVM picks G1 only on what it calls a server-class machine: at least 2 CPUs and at least 1,792 MB of memory, both as the JVM sees them inside a container. Anything smaller silently gets Serial, HotSpot's simplest collector: one GC thread does all the work while every application thread waits. (Parallel does the same with many GC threads.) A small helper program next to the thumbnail service, in a container with 1 CPU or a 1 GiB memory limit, has run Serial all along unless someone named a collector. Per the JDK 27 source, JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere.

Then ask what hurts most. If long pauses hurt, because a person waits on every request, look at the low-pause crews. If total work per CPU hurts, because a job runs for hours and nobody waits on one step, look at Parallel. If memory hurts, because the container is small, remember that concurrent crews need headroom. These are my starting points, not benchmark results:

Collector The crew Pick it when Watch out for
Serial one cleaner, pens down 1 CPU and a heap up to a few hundred MB full GCs that grow with the live data
Parallel many cleaners, pens down batch jobs, where total time beats any single pause long pauses on big heaps
G1 the crew with a stopwatch, from lesson 4 most services: heaps from about 256 MB to tens of GB, pause budgets of tens of milliseconds Evacuation Failure, Pause Full, many arrays over half a region
ZGC moves boxes while the workers work pause budgets under about 10 ms, with cores to spare CPU in small containers, Allocation Stall, 8-byte references
Shenandoah the same goal, another design the same goals as ZGC, on a JDK that includes it availability; generational mode only from JDK 24
Epsilon never cleans at all tests and benchmarks only the JVM stops when the heap is full, by design

The flags change with the JDK:

Collector JDK 21 JDK 25
G1, Serial, Parallel -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:+UseSerialGC, -XX:+UseParallelGC the same
Generational ZGC -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -XX:+UseZGC
Generational Shenandoah not available -XX:+UseShenandoahGC -XX:ShenandoahGCMode=generational
Epsilon -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC the same

When you move a program from JDK 21 to 25, take -XX:+ZGenerational out. JDK 25 starts anyway and says so: Ignoring option ZGenerational; support was removed in 24.0. Pick a collector by the bill you can least afford, then watch the log for that bill. The lab turns both tables into code.

One row in the first table looks like a joke: a crew that never cleans. In a test, it's the most honest collector there is.

sections.h: A crew that never cleans: Epsilon as an allocation budget
sections.html:
Epsilon is a collector that never collects. It hands out memory, and when the heap is full, the JVM stops:

Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space

Epsilon is a cleaning crew that never shows up. In a running service, that's a short career. In a test, it's a measuring tool, because under Epsilon the heap size becomes an allocation budget: if a piece of code finishes under -Xmx64m, a heap of at most 64 MB, it allocated less than 64 MB in total, a few of which went to starting the JVM.

The demo puts lesson 2's upload report on that budget. It adds up the bytes that each of 500 users uploaded, over 5 million uploads, in two versions. Each version runs in its own JVM with Epsilon and a 64 MB heap. The long[] version finishes. The Map<Integer, Long> version dies. It dies even though the JIT's escape analysis (lesson 2's trick of skipping objects that never leave a method) may remove the temporary boxes for the key and the size, because every running sum is a new 24-byte Long that the map stores. Epsilon frees none of the old ones, and 5 million of them need at least 120 MB.

Epsilon has two other honest uses: benchmarks that must not be disturbed by GC pauses, and very short jobs that finish before they could fill the heap.

It's an experimental option on every JDK from 21 to 27, and the JVM is fussy about the order of its flags. Write -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions, and JDK 25 refuses to start:

Error: VM option 'UseEpsilonGC' is experimental and must be enabled via -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions.
Error: The unlock option must precede 'UseEpsilonGC'.

So the experimental switch comes first, and the collector after it. Epsilon makes its bill obvious by failing. The other collectors write theirs into the GC log, quietly, one line at a time.

try.title: Put the upload report on an allocation budget
steps: Read EpsilonDemo. Each version runs in a child JVM with Epsilon and a 64 MB heap.
Predict which version finishes, then run it.
Change UPLOADS to 1,000,000 and run it again, then to 2,000,000. Does the point where the boxed version breaks match 24 bytes per upload?

code.title: EpsilonDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.memory.l05; import workbench.memory.Jvm; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of lesson 2's * upload report (the bytes each user uploaded) run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ public class EpsilonDemo { static final int UPLOADS = 5_000_000, USERS = 500; static long boxedTotals() { Map<Integer, Long> totals = new HashMap<>(); // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per upload, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the size for (int i = 0; i < UPLOADS; i++) totals.merge(i % USERS, 1_000L + i % 9_000, Long::sum); return totals.values().stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum(); } static long primitiveTotals() { long[] totals = new long[USERS]; for (int i = 0; i < UPLOADS; i++) totals[i % USERS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000; // no objects long sum = 0; for (long t : totals) sum += t; return sum; } public static void main(String[] args) { if (args.length > 0) { long sum = args[0].equals("boxed") ? boxedTotals() : primitiveTotals(); System.out.println("finished inside the budget, total " + sum); return; } List<String> epsilon = List.of("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m"); for (String version : List.of("primitive", "boxed")) { System.out.println("== " + version); Jvm.lines(epsilon, EpsilonDemo.class.getName(), version).forEach(System.out::println); } } }

alt.title: EpsilonDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.memory.l05 import workbench.memory.Jvm private const val UPLOADS = 5_000_000 private const val USERS = 500 private fun boxedTotals(): Long { val totals = HashMap<Int, Long>() // every sum is a new Long stored in the map: at least 24 bytes per upload, even when the JIT // removes the temporary boxes for the key and the size for (i in 0 until UPLOADS) totals.merge(i % USERS, 1_000L + i % 9_000) { a, b -> a + b } return totals.values.sum() } private fun primitiveTotals(): Long { val totals = LongArray(USERS) for (i in 0 until UPLOADS) totals[i % USERS] += 1_000L + i % 9_000 // no objects return totals.sum() } /** * Epsilon never frees anything, so a heap of 64 MB is an allocation budget. Two versions of lesson 2's * upload report (the bytes each user uploaded) run against that budget, each in its own child JVM. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.isNotEmpty()) { val sum = if (args[0] == "boxed") boxedTotals() else primitiveTotals() println("finished inside the budget, total $sum") return } val epsilon = listOf("-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions", "-XX:+UseEpsilonGC", "-Xmx64m") for (version in listOf("primitive", "boxed")) { println("== $version") Jvm.lines(epsilon, "workbench.memory.l05.EpsilonDemoKt", version).forEach(::println) } }

try.expect: primitive prints finished inside the budget, total 27487500000. boxed prints Terminating due to java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space: five million new Long sums need at least 120 MB, and nothing is ever freed. On JDK 25, the boxed version finished with 1,000,000 uploads (at least 24 MB of sums) and failed every time with 2,000,000 (at least 48 MB, plus the JVM's own start-up and any temporary boxes the JIT didn't remove). A budget test should leave a wide margin for exactly that reason.

compare.title: Report which collector runs, from inside the program

java.title: GcReport.java
java.html: // print once at startup, and on a timer if you like for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { System.out.printf("%s: %d collections, %d ms%n", gc.getName(), gc.getCollectionCount(), gc.getCollectionTime()); }

kotlin.title: GcReport.kt
kotlin.html: // print once at startup, and on a timer if you like ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans().forEach { gc -> println("${gc.name}: ${gc.collectionCount} collections, ${gc.collectionTime} ms") }

compare.note: Both versions call the same JDK API; Kotlin reads the getters as properties and puts the values straight into a string template. What differs is what the beans mean for each collector, as JDK 25 names them. G1 reports G1 Young Generation, G1 Concurrent GC and G1 Old Generation. ZGC reports ZGC Minor Cycles, ZGC Minor Pauses, ZGC Major Cycles and ZGC Major Pauses, and Shenandoah reports Shenandoah Pauses and Shenandoah Cycles. The time of a "Cycles" bean is concurrent work, not stopped time. A chart that adds up every bean's time as "GC pause" makes ZGC look like the slowest collector of all, the same trap as reading the 0.071 s in its log as a pause.

worked.title: Pick collectors for three programs of the photo site

steps.say: Three programs, three sets of facts. The thumbnail service: 4 CPUs, a 2 GB heap, and a latency target that leaves about 100 ms for GC. A photo search service: 8 CPUs at 30% use, a 16 GB heap of cached search data, and a 5 ms GC budget. A nightly job that re-encodes every photo: 8 CPUs, 16 GB, and nobody waiting on any single photo. Write them down as Workloads, the lab's record for what a JVM has to run.
steps.code: var thumbnails = new Workload(Workload.Kind.SERVICE, 4, 2_048, 100); var search = new Workload(Workload.Kind.SERVICE, 8, 16_384, 5); var nightly = new Workload(Workload.Kind.BATCH, 8, 16_384, 5_000);

steps.say: 1. The thumbnail service keeps G1. Its log shows young pauses of 10 to 20 ms, far inside the 100 ms budget. If it ever shows (Evacuation Failure: Allocation) or Pause Full, the answer is more heap headroom, not another collector.

1. The search service moves to ZGC. Its 5 ms budget is below what G1 can promise on a 16 GB heap, and it has cores to spare. The flags depend on the JDK, so take them from the table, not from an old page you found online. Then decide what to watch after the switch.
steps.code:
JDK 21:  -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx16g
JDK 25:  -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx16g

watch:   pause lines in -Xlog:gc*          (expect well under 1 ms)
         'Allocation Stall' in the GC log   (expect none)
         CPU of the container               (expect it to rise a little)
         heap use                           (references are now 8 bytes)

steps.say: 1. The nightly job gets Parallel. It only cares how soon the whole run finishes, and Parallel's longer pauses bother nobody. Check all three against the lab's decision function, which holds the same table.

lab.title: Turn the collector tables into code
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail. Collector and Workload are given: an enum of the collectors and a record for what a JVM has to run.
Write defaultCollector: G1 from JDK 27; before that, G1 only with 2 or more CPUs and at least 1,792 MB, otherwise Serial.

Write flagsFor with a switch over the collector. Add -XX:+ZGenerational for ZGC before JDK 23. Throw IllegalArgumentException for generational Shenandoah before JDK 24. Put -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions first wherever it's needed: for Epsilon always, and for generational Shenandoah on JDK 24.
Write recommend as the five rows of the decision table in its Javadoc, in order.
Run the tests until all seven pass. Then describe a program of your own as a Workload and see whether you agree with the answer.
hints: 1,792 MB is 2 GB minus 256 MB. The test uses 1,791 and 1,792 to check the boundary.
Return List.copyOf(flags) so callers can't change your list.
In recommend, the order of the rows matters: a 1-CPU batch job with a 256 MB heap gets Serial, because that row comes first.

drill.title: Write the flags from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page. Write the JVM flags for generational ZGC on JDK 21 and on JDK 25, and for Epsilon on JDK 25. Then say which collector a JDK 25 program gets with no GC flag in a container with 2 CPUs and a 1.5 GiB memory limit. Finally, write defaultCollector from memory.

answer.html: // ZGC on 21: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational // ZGC on 25: -XX:+UseZGC // Epsilon: -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC (the experimental switch first) // 2 CPUs, 1.5 GiB = 1,536 MB < 1,792 MB: not server-class, so Serial (G1 on JDK 27) static Collector defaultCollector(int jdk, int cpus, long memoryMb) { if (jdk >= 27) return Collector.G1; return cpus >= 2 && memoryMb >= 1_792 ? Collector.G1 : Collector.SERIAL; }

alt.html: // ZGC on 21: -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational // ZGC on 25: -XX:+UseZGC // Epsilon: -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGC (the experimental switch first) // 2 CPUs, 1.5 GiB = 1,536 MB < 1,792 MB: not server-class, so Serial (G1 on JDK 27) fun defaultCollector(jdk: Int, cpus: Int, memoryMb: Long): Collector = when { jdk >= 27 -> Collector.G1 cpus >= 2 && memoryMb >= 1_792 -> Collector.G1 else -> Collector.SERIAL }

recap: ZGC moves objects while threads run. Colored references and a load barrier on every reference load let a thread repair a stale reference itself, so the pauses only switch phases and stay around hundredths of a millisecond at any heap size.
In a ZGC log, the time on a Minor Collection or Major Collection line is the concurrent collection. The pauses are the Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End and Pause Relocate Start lines.

Generational ZGC: opt-in on JDK 21 (-XX:+ZGenerational), the default on 23, the only mode from 24. Shenandoah is the other concurrent collector; its generational mode is experimental on 24 and a product feature on 25.

With no GC flag, JDK 21 to 26 pick Serial unless the JVM sees 2 CPUs and 1,792 MB; JDK 27 picks G1 everywhere. Keep G1 for most services, ZGC for tight pause budgets with spare cores, Parallel for batch jobs, Epsilon for allocation-budget tests.
Epsilon never frees memory, so a heap size becomes an allocation budget. Put -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions first.

The limit of low pauses: the work moves out of the pause, not out of the program. It comes back as CPU for GC threads and barriers, as headroom (or allocation stalls when there's too little), and, for ZGC, as 8-byte references.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks: "Why don't we just use ZGC everywhere? It has the shortest pauses." Answer in your own words: how ZGC gets its short pauses, what it costs, and how you would decide for each program.
explain.answer: ZGC moves objects while the application runs. Every reference in the heap carries color bits, and a load barrier after each reference load checks them; if a reference is stale, the thread repairs it on the spot. So the pauses only switch the collector from one phase to the next, and they stay well under a millisecond whatever the heap size. The cost moves elsewhere. GC threads use CPU beside the request threads, the barrier runs on every load, the heap needs headroom because the application keeps allocating during a collection (or threads stall), and references take 8 bytes, so objects get bigger. I'd decide from each program's GC log. If G1's real pauses fit the latency budget, stay on G1. If they don't, and the container has spare cores, try ZGC and watch CPU, allocation stalls and heap use.

deeper.html:
The full -Xlog:gc* output of one ZGC minor collection on JDK 25 has more to read than the pause lines. These come from the same run as the lesson's log, trimmed:

GC(3) Using 1 Workers for Young Generation
GC(3) y: Allocation Stalls:          0                0                0                0
GC(3) y: Load: 26.33 (658%) / 23.99 (600%) / 24.50 (612%)
GC(3) y: MMU: 2ms/98.4%, 5ms/99.1%, 10ms/99.4%, 20ms/99.5%, 50ms/99.8%, 100ms/99.9%
GC(3) y: Eden              43M (4%)          770M (75%)        375 / 350            2 / 0              0 / 0
GC(3) y: Allocated:         -                16M (2%)           22M (2%)          100M (10%)

Using 1 Workers means ZGC chose one GC thread for this collection; the count is dynamic. Load is the machine's load average, here over six times its 4 cores: the busy machine this lesson keeps mentioning. MMU is minimum mutator utilization: 2ms/98.4% means that in every 2 ms window of this collection, the application got at least 98.4% of the time. It's a better latency number than pause length alone, because it also catches several pauses close together. The Eden row is lesson 4's generational hypothesis again: 43 MB live against 770 MB of garbage. Allocated is the headroom bill from section 2: 100 MB of new objects by the end of the collection. Allocation Stalls should stay all zeros.

A prefix tells you which generation a line is about: y: for the young collection of a minor GC, Y: and O: for the young and old parts of a major GC.

ZGC also gives memory back to the operating system on its own. ZUncommit is on by default and returns memory that has been unused for ZUncommitDelay, 300 seconds by default. G1 can shrink its heap after a full GC, and its periodic collection for idle programs is off by default (G1PeriodicGCInterval is 0). That difference can matter in a container: a ZGC program's memory can fall after a busy spell, while a G1 program may keep what it grew to.
